ch04.title: The Day of Ordination
ch04.b002: At Bethsaida the winter morning came first to the water. While the far hills across the lake turned from ash gray to a pale, watery blue, Andrew drew the net that hung over the gunwale into his lap and felt his way along it, mesh by mesh, searching out the torn places. The cords had drunk the night dew and gone stiff, and each time he pushed the bone needle through, his cold fingertips ached. Peter was fishing in the shallows close to the beach, casting and hauling, while Andrew sat in the boat and mended. Neither of them had gone out far from shore that morning. No one had decided it. But for days a single thought had lodged in every one of their chests, the thought that the call might come at any hour, and it had made each man tie his boat close to land.
ch04.b003: It was Sunday, January 12, A.D. 27. Since the summer before, when the twelve had first been bound together into one company, they had lived by a steady rhythm: two weeks of fishing, then two weeks going out two by two among the villages of Galilee. Those five months and more had been quiet, and at times monotonous. There had been no standing before crowds, no crying out the kingdom in a loud voice from a synagogue floor. Yet in the last few days something had changed in the Master’s eyes. It was the look of a man who has carried something for a long while and is choosing the moment to set it down. Andrew had seen it, and he supposed the others had seen it too, each in his own fashion.
ch04.b004: He was the chief of the apostolic corps. Nobody said the word much aloud, but when anything happened, every eye went first to Andrew. Who was to go to which village, whose house had sickness in it, whether the purse would stretch to the end of the week: he kept all of it spread out in his mind like a map laid on a table. This morning too, while his hands went on knotting the mesh, his thoughts went around the faces of the other eleven, one after another. Peter would talk a great deal today. The two sons of Zebedee would act, beside their father, as though nothing at all were happening. Philip would be counting what they needed to bring, and Thomas would be counting what might go wrong.
ch04.b005: And Judas. Andrew’s needle stopped. Judas Iscariot was a treasurer beyond reproach. His accounts were clean and his reckoning was quick, and no one else could have brought such order to the haphazard affairs of a band of Galilean fishermen. And yet, every so often, Andrew felt something slide sideways beneath all that neatness: when a smile arrived a moment late, when a word of agreement ended a little too short. He had no name for it. So he told no one. It was not his way to speak of a thing he was not sure of.
ch04.b007: Peter had waded up alongside the boat, laughing. Andrew looked down. It was true. He cut the thread without a word. Peter was used to his brother’s silences. If the younger brother’s words ran ahead of his thoughts, the elder’s thoughts ran a long way ahead of his words. Thirty-three and thirty, older and younger, they had lived that way for years, each filling in what the other lacked. Andrew often wanted to say something warm to his brother, but such words always lingered somewhere in his throat and then were gone. Praise, to him, stood too close to flattery.
ch04.b008: Then he saw a man walking along the water’s edge. It was nearly noon. The sunlight was thin but clear, and the footprints in the wet sand stood out sharply. The walk was unhurried, yet there was no hesitation in it. Andrew stood up in the boat. Peter was already turning, knee-deep in the lake, his face lifted toward the shore.
ch04.b009: The Master hailed the two brothers first. Not many words were needed. Then he signaled to James and John, who were in a boat a little way off, visiting with their father, Zebedee, and mending nets. Zebedee laid down the net in his hands and looked at his two sons. Andrew could not read all that passed across the old fisherman’s face. Pride, perhaps, or a quiet grief. Probably both. Zebedee had already given his large house over to Jesus and the twelve. Today he was giving the rest of what he had, his two sons.
ch04.b011: Two by two the Master gathered up the other apostles. Peter followed behind him with a heart fit to burst. Today, at last. For weeks, no, for months, he had been waiting for this day: the day the kingdom would be proclaimed, the day they would stop being nameless men going back and forth between their fishing boats and the village lanes. He wanted to say something, anything. What would happen today? Where were they going? What ought they to bring? When it came to questions, Peter had more than the other eleven put together.
ch04.b012: And yet a strange thing happened. Each time he opened his mouth, something held his tongue. The back of the man walking ahead of him looked no different from any other day: the worn cloak, the strong shoulders, the hair stirred a little by the wind off the lake. But as he watched that back, Peter felt the words inside him sink, one after another, to the bottom. He walked on in silence. He could not remember the last time he had walked so far without speaking.
ch04.b013: Philip joined them where the lane came down into Bethsaida. He had a small sack slung on his back: a few barley loaves, some dried fish, a skin of water. He was the steward of the apostolic family, and worrying about where and what thirteen men would eat was his work. Whatever kind of day this turned out to be, men would get hungry. That was the law of the world as Philip understood it. He retied the cord of the sack and did his sums. Until sundown this would be plenty. If they went on into the night, it would not be enough. But the sack was not opened once before the sun went down. Philip noticed it only later, and smiled a little to himself.
ch04.b014: Nathaniel walked close at Philip’s elbow. This young man from Cana was twenty-five, younger than anyone but John. He glanced at Philip’s sack and lowered his voice.
ch04.b015: “Philip, I take it even ambassadors of the kingdom eat lunch?”
ch04.b016: Philip did not answer, but the corner of his mouth twitched. Nathaniel looked ahead, satisfied. He loved philosophy and he loved to dream, and between the two he loved to slip in some odd joke. The more solemn the moment, the more he itched to make one; it was an old habit of his. But today even he said nothing more. A joke was for loosening a tight moment, not for breaking a reverent one.
ch04.b017: The twins were waiting, sitting side by side on a rock by the water. James and Judas, the sons of Alpheus, had the same face, the same build, the same laugh. You had to look a long while to tell which was which, and in truth there was seldom any need. Whatever could be said of one could be said of the other almost word for word. When they saw the Master coming, they stood up together and brushed the sand from their clothes together. No one had to explain to them at length what day this was. The Master had called, and so they went. That was enough.
ch04.b019: When all twelve were together, they climbed into the highlands north of Capernaum. Once the path left the lakeside villages behind, it quickly grew steep. Winter grass showed green between the stones, and here and there a black lump of basalt sat in the slope like something left behind by a giant. As their breath came harder, the company drew out into a long line of its own accord. In front walked the Master with Peter, James, and John, the three who early on had been set to attend him day and night. The rest followed, each at his own pace.
ch04.b020: Matthew Levi walked near the back. He had not meant to, but whenever he came to himself, he found he was at the tail of the line. In the days when he sat in the customs house at Capernaum, people had either lowered their eyes before his table or glared at it. The name of publican had clung to his family for a long time. None of the twelve despised him openly. But in the first months it had taken time, especially for Simon Zelotes and Judas Iscariot, before they could sit easily in the same room with him. Matthew had borne that time without complaint.
ch04.b021: He had a secret that no one knew. No one but the Master. Whenever the apostolic purse ran low, whenever the expected offerings fell short, he quietly drew on his own means and filled the gap. Often he gave in the names of other believers, because he feared his companions might think a publican’s money unclean. When he met a look of disdain, he burned to tell them: Do you know whose money bought the bread you ate yesterday? But he never once said it. He would not say it today either. Only the wish that the Master might know, that wish he had never been able to put down.
ch04.b022: Ahead he could see Simon Zelotes taking the slope in long, rough strides. Matthew knew that kind of man well. In his years at the customs table, Zealots like Simon had called him Rome’s dog. That he and such a man were now climbing the same path together still struck Matthew as a wonder. Faith alone is needed in this business of finding God, he told himself. It was the name he liked best for this company and its work: this business of finding God.
ch04.b023: Simon did not feel Matthew’s eyes on him. His head was crowded with other things. Today. He was sure of it. For five months the Master had been far too quiet. John the Baptist still lay in Herod’s prison; Roman soldiers still stood at the crossroads of Galilee. Simon had given up a high office among the Zealots to become an apostle. His old comrades had called him a traitor, and some had called him mad. He had told them to wait. This man is different, he had said.
ch04.b024: He was twenty-eight, a fiery agitator. His words ran ahead of his thoughts, and his anger ran ahead of his words. The freedom of Israel was a dream that flowed in his blood. Each time the Master healed and taught, Simon believed it was the beginning of something greater. Whoever won the hearts of the people would win the nation in the end. Whatever the Master proclaimed on the mountain today, it would surely concern that nation. Simon clenched his fist and opened it again. His palm was wet.
ch04.b025: Judas Iscariot walked somewhere between the two of them. He felt the weight of the purse at his belt. He remembered to the coin what it had held when he counted it that morning; that was his habit, to keep a tally of everything, men and money and chances alike. He looked at the backs of the three men walking ahead. Peter, James, John. Galilean fishermen. Always at the Master’s side. At the night vigils of prayer, at the conversations no one else heard, they were there. It was Andrew who had chosen them for those places, when the Master asked him to name two or three to stay by his side. Judas sometimes wondered whether it had been fair.
ch04.b026: He was the only Judean among the twelve. Born in Kerioth in southern Judea and raised in Jericho, he had been disowned by his Sadducee parents when he followed John the Baptist. He was probably the best-educated man in the company. He had never paraded it, but he had never forgotten it either. When he first met the Master at the landing in Tarichea, the Master had told him that they were all of one flesh, and that he prayed Judas would always be loyal to his Galilean brethren. Judas often thought of those words. They had been words of welcome. Why, then, did their ending sometimes sound to him like a warning?
ch04.b027: He remembered something else. On the Sabbath evening when the twelve first gathered at Zebedee’s house, he had drawn the Master aside and asked him why nothing was being done to get John out of prison. The answer had not satisfied him. Ever since, he had carried a small doubt in a corner of his heart: could this man be timid, a little afraid to assert his own power? But today might be different. If the Master at last showed that power today, then Judas must be among those standing beside him when he did. So Judas reckoned.
ch04.b028: As they neared the top, something unusual happened. No one spoke. For once all twelve of them were silent. Even Peter was lost in thought. There was only the wind, the crunch of gravel underfoot, the breathing of thirteen men. Each had climbed with a different hope, but the silence they shared was one silence. The long-awaited hour was coming at last.
ch04.b030: At the top was a grassy hollow where the wind dropped away. Looking south, they could see the Sea of Galilee glittering like fish scales under the winter sun, and the white roofs of Capernaum huddled at the water’s edge. A few small fishing boats rode on the lake, the very boats they themselves had been sitting in that morning. The Master sat down in the middle of the grass, and the twelve sat around him.
ch04.b031: He called them his brethren. He told them that the hour of the kingdom had come, and that he had brought them apart to this place to present them to the Father as its ambassadors. Some of them had first heard him speak of the kingdom in the synagogue when they were called, and since then, working with him in the towns around the lake, every one of them had learned more. But now he had something further to tell them.
ch04.b032: Thomas Didymus leaned his elbows on his knees and listened. He was not a man who heard words so much as one who took them apart. A sentence came in, and he turned it, flipped it over, and set it against what he had heard before. He had once been a carpenter and a stone mason. Stone does not lie. If it is cracked, it is cracked; if it is out of true, it is out of true. He wished to handle words in the same way. But this man’s words were not like stone. Measure them as often as he liked, he could never find where they ended.
ch04.b033: The Master said that the new kingdom his Father was about to set up in the hearts of his children on earth would be a dominion without end. He told them that his Father was the God of neither Jew nor gentile. Many would come from the east and from the west to sit down together in that kingdom, he said, while many of Abraham’s own children would refuse to come in.
ch04.b034: Nathaniel’s face stiffened. He was proud of his family, of his town, of his nation. That pride was both his virtue and his snare. It was the same pride that had asked, before he ever met Jesus, whether any good thing could come out of Nazareth. But it had also been Nathaniel who, after one look into that face, turned his opinion around. He was proud, but he was not obstinate. A kingdom where gentiles sat at the table. He tried to picture it. It was strange. And yet, oddly, he did not dislike it.
ch04.b035: Judas Iscariot heard the same words differently. If the Father was the God of the gentiles too, then what became of David’s throne? What of the restoration of Israel? He did not put the question into words. He entered it instead in the ledger of his mind: an item not understood.
ch04.b036: The Master said that the power of this kingdom would lie not in the strength of armies or the might of riches, but in the glory of the divine spirit, which would come to teach the minds and govern the hearts of the sons of God. It would be a brotherhood of love in which righteousness reigned, he said, and its battle cry would be peace on earth and good will to all men.
ch04.b037: Simon Zelotes held his breath. Not in the strength of armies. He repeated it to himself, once, twice. But almost at once he found a way to read it otherwise. Not yet; that must be what it meant. First the hearts, and afterward. He soothed himself. Peace on earth. To a Zealot, peace came only after victory. That a day would come when he himself would go about preaching exactly that peace and that good will, Simon could not have dreamed that afternoon.
ch04.b038: At the words “the might of riches,” Matthew lowered his eyes. He knew better than anyone what riches could do. And he was beginning, little by little, to learn what they could not do. The Master told them what their message to the world was to be: they should seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and every other thing needed for eternal survival would come along with it.
ch04.b039: And then he made it plain. This kingdom would not arrive with an outward display of power or with any unseemly demonstration. They were not to go about saying that it was here, or that it was there. For the kingdom they would preach was God within them.
ch04.b040: Thomas looked up. God within. He took the phrase into his hand and weighed it. How could you carry to others a thing that could not be seen? How could you ask men to believe what could not be proved? But he also thought back over the past five months, over the things he had watched at this man’s side. The way he treated people, the way he never lost his temper, the way he never hurried. That was not proof. But it was evidence. Thomas knew the difference.
ch04.b041: The Master said that whoever would be great in his Father’s kingdom must become a minister to all, and whoever would be first among them must become the servant of his brothers. John Zebedee’s face grew warm as he listened. He was twenty-four, the youngest of the twelve. He had been the youngest at home and he was the youngest here. And he was one of the three at the Master’s side. In secret he was proud of it. He believed he hid that pride well. But these words seemed aimed straight at him.
ch04.b042: The kingdom, the Master said, would go forward in the world until it had broken down every barrier. And some of those sitting there, he told them, would not die before they had seen the reign of God come in great power.
ch04.b043: Peter’s eyes lit up. Simon Zelotes’s fist closed again. Great power. They had heard the same words and seen the same picture. Both of them were wrong, and on that day the only one who knew it was the one speaking.
ch04.b044: The Master raised his hand toward them. What their eyes now looked upon, he said, this small beginning of twelve commonplace men, would multiply and grow until at last the whole earth was filled with the praise of his Father.
ch04.b045: Twelve commonplace men. Nathaniel very nearly laughed. He looked around the circle of faces. Fishermen with cracked hands, a steward who knew only how to count, a publican, a Zealot, a gloomy stone mason, and those twins. Commonplace indeed. It would be hard to be more so. And yet the word did not sound like an insult at all. If anything it sounded like the most astonishing part of the whole affair: that heaven had chosen such ordinary vessels.
ch04.b046: The twins took the word just as it came. Commonplace was what they had been called all their lives, and it was not untrue. They were the only apostles who had never been through the synagogue schools. They understood half of the Master’s deeper sayings, sometimes less. And today the Master had called that very commonness a beginning. The twins did not look at each other, but at the same moment the same warmth rose in both their chests.
ch04.b047: Last of all the Master told them that men would know they had been with him, and had learned the realities of the kingdom, less by the words they spoke than by the lives they lived. He had no wish, he said, to lay heavy burdens on their minds; but he was about to lay on their souls the solemn charge of representing him in the world when, before long, he would leave them.
ch04.b048: When before long he would leave them. Those words caught in Andrew’s ear. In John’s, too. The others let them pass by. No one on that hillside could have understood what they meant. When he had finished speaking, the Master stood up.
ch04.b050: He told the twelve to kneel in a circle around him. They knelt on the grass. The cold of the winter ground came through the cloth and into their knees. Someone’s breath was trembling. There was no telling whose.
ch04.b051: The first head on which the Master laid his hands was the head of Judas Iscariot.
ch04.b052: Judas felt the weight. They were a carpenter’s hands, thick at the joints, hard in the palm, and warmer than he had expected. While they rested on his head, everything that had been reckoning inside him stopped for a moment: the ledger, the purse, the backs of the three men ahead on the path. He felt nothing but the weight of those hands. Strangely, it was not heavy. It was more like a hand that was lifting something up.
ch04.b053: When the hands left him, the reckoning began again. Why me first? he thought. Did it mean first in honor? What could it mean, to set apart first the man who had come in last? He wanted to read it as a distinction. But another voice whispered inside him: Or does he begin with the one he worries about most? Judas pushed that voice away. But he could not push it all the way out.
ch04.b054: The hands moved around the circle, one man at a time.
ch04.b055: When the hands came to rest on Thomas, he kept his eyes closed and tried to measure something. What is happening? What is changing? But there was nothing to measure. Instead, without warning, he thought of his twin sister, lost when he was nine years old. He did not know why she came to him now. Since she died he had become a man who doubted first, because the world could take away the dearest thing at any moment. But the hands on his head now were not hands that took. That much Thomas knew for certain, though he could not have proved it. He fixed the weight and warmth of those hands in his memory; measuring a thing and keeping a record of it was his way. One day, after everything had fallen apart, in a room with its doors barred, he would face these hands again, and on that day he would search them for evidence. But that day was far off, and no one yet knew of it.
ch04.b056: When the hands rested on Matthew, his whole body went rigid. On the head of the man whose hands had sat at a customs table, had counted coins, had been spat upon, these hands now lay. He felt that they did not hesitate. They stayed exactly as long as they had stayed on every other head. Not a moment less. To Matthew that was everything. He held back his tears.
ch04.b057: As the hands came down on Simon Zelotes, he clenched his jaw, as if bracing for a blow. But the hands offered no fight. They were not hands that pressed a sword into his grip. They simply stayed. Simon felt something in him loosen a little, and that frightened him.
ch04.b058: When the hands rested on the twins, neither of them thought anything at all. That was their blessing. In that moment they were simply there. The Master had put his hands on their heads. That was enough.
ch04.b059: Philip, even then, tried to take hold of something. Show me: that was his habit. But this time there was nothing to be shown. There were only hands on his head. And yet Philip remembered that those hands had always been generous. Never once had he found anything small or stingy in this man. The memory held him steady.
ch04.b060: Nathaniel did not think of a joke. It was the first time.
ch04.b061: Under the weight of the hands, John thought of long ago. He and his brother James had known this man longer than any of the others. John had looked after the affairs of this man’s mother and brothers. He knew how faithfully the man had cared for his family even while he wandered without a home. And now that same man had his hands on John’s head. For the first time, John was ashamed of his pride.
ch04.b062: James Zebedee was quiet when the hands rested on him. He was a man whose talkative days took turns with silent ones, and this was a silent day. But this silence was not his usual unaccountable kind. It was a silence filled to the brim.
ch04.b063: When the hands came down on Peter, he felt that he was about to burst into tears. He had never learned to master strong feeling. When he was glad he laughed, when he was angry he shouted, when he was sad he wept. But this once he made no sound. If he made a sound beneath those hands, it seemed to him, something would break. Instead his shoulders shook. He thought: A man like me. A man who speaks before he thinks, who overturns at night what he resolved in the morning. And these hands rested on such a man for just as long as on any other. The gratitude was more than he could hold. And silently he swore an oath: Whatever happens, I will never leave these hands. How heavy that oath would turn out to be, the Peter of that day did not know.
ch04.b064: And last of all, the hands rested on Andrew’s head. The first to be called was the last to be blessed. Andrew did not find that strange. The chief is always the one who checks last, making sure everyone is safe and no one has been left out. Beneath those hands he thought about the work ahead of him. Once more he went through the faces of the other eleven in turn. And at the very first face, the face of Judas, his thoughts paused.
ch04.b065: Then, all at once, Andrew felt again the hands upon his own head. He was always the one watching over others: who was tired, who was missing, who was wavering. But now someone was watching over him. Not because he was the chief, not because he had been the first one called, but simply because he was Andrew. Only in that moment did he understand how long he had been waiting for it. Thirty-three years as the eldest son, as head of a fatherless household, as the guardian of a younger brother, as chief of the twelve; and from the stiff shoulders of that man something quietly settled and came to rest. Andrew did not weep. He only kept his eyes closed a long while.
ch04.b066: When he had blessed them all, the Master stretched out his hands and prayed. He told the Father that he was bringing to him these men, his messengers. From among the children of earth he had chosen these twelve to go out and represent him, as he had come out to represent the Father. He asked the Father to love them and be with them, as the Father had loved him and been with him. He was placing all the affairs of the coming kingdom in their hands, he said, and he asked that they be given wisdom. If it was the Father’s will, he would stay on earth a while longer to help them in their labors. And at the last he gave thanks for these men, and he entrusted them to the Father’s keeping while he went on to finish the work the Father had given him to do.
ch04.b067: The prayer ended. No one moved. Each apostle stayed bowed where he knelt. Many minutes passed before even Peter dared to raise his eyes to the Master’s face. Then, one by one, they rose and embraced him. No one said a word. No word was needed, and no word was possible.
ch04.b068: Simon Zelotes embraced him hard and roughly, the way a fighter embraces a comrade, and the Master received that rough embrace just as it came. The twins came forward almost together, then hesitated, each stepping back to let the other go first. The Master opened both arms and held them both at once. Matthew hung back until the very last. Whether a publican might be the one to step forward, he still was not sure. So the Master went to him and took him in his arms. Inside that embrace, for the first time, Matthew wept without a sound. Judas Iscariot embraced the Master too. The Master’s arms held him neither more briefly nor longer than they had held anyone else. How unchanging that embrace had been, the eleven would ponder for a long time afterward.
ch04.b069: A great silence lay over the highland. Unseen by their eyes, a host of heavenly beings was looking down upon the scene: the Creator of a universe placing the work of the divine brotherhood of man into the hands of ordinary men.
ch04.b071: Then the Master spoke again. Now that they were ambassadors of his Father’s kingdom, he said, they could no longer live as they had lived before. From this hour they must live like men who had tasted the glories of a better world and had been sent back to earth as its ambassadors. More was expected of the teacher than of the pupil, he said, and more of the master than of the servant. And some of the things he was about to tell them, he warned, would sound hard.
ch04.b072: He was sending them out, he said, to proclaim liberty to those held captive in spirit and joy to those bound by fear, and to heal the sick. And when they found his children in distress, they were to encourage them with words such as these: that the poor in spirit, the humble, were happy; and those who hungered and thirsted for righteousness; and the meek; and the pure in heart.
ch04.b073: The twins understood those words more easily than anyone. They had always known what hunger was, and what meekness was. For them these things were not philosophy but something more like the weather. And such people were happy? One of the twins nodded, very slightly. The other nodded too.
ch04.b074: Those who mourned, the Master went on, would be comforted. The merciful would obtain mercy. The peacemakers would be called the sons of God. Those who were persecuted for righteousness’ sake were happy, he said, and when men reviled them and hounded them and falsely spoke every kind of evil against them, they should rejoice and be glad.
ch04.b075: At the word peacemakers, something in James Zebedee caught. Once his anger was roused, he could not rein it in; and when the storm had passed, he always excused it to himself as righteous indignation. Peacemakers. He held on to the word a long time. At the word merciful, Matthew bowed his head. He had received mercy. He knew how it tasted.
ch04.b076: The Master told them that they were the salt of the earth. But if the salt lost its savor, he asked, what could make it salty again? It would be good for nothing then but to be thrown out and trodden underfoot.
ch04.b077: At the word salt, Philip’s ears pricked up. Here was something he knew. Salt was costly. It was even used in place of money. It cured meat, preserved fish, and gave bread its taste. In the fish-drying sheds of Bethsaida he had learned how precious a single sack of salt could be. Salt that had lost its savor was useless indeed. Philip liked the figure. For the first time, one of the Master’s great sayings seemed to be something he could hold in his hand.
ch04.b078: The Master told them that they were the light of the world. A city set on a hill could not be hidden. No one lit a lamp and put it under a bushel; they set it on a stand, and it lit the whole house. So their light was to shine before men, that men might see their good works and be led to glorify their Father in heaven.
ch04.b079: Nathaniel looked down the southern slope. Capernaum sat white in the sunlight. It was no city set on a hill, but this highland could surely be seen from its streets. And these twelve men who had knelt on this hill were to be the light of that town. He found the thought both laughable and beautiful.
ch04.b080: The Master’s words grew harder. They were not to resist injustice by force, he said, nor to trust in the arm of the flesh. If a neighbor struck them on the right cheek, they should turn the other one to him as well. Rather than go to law among themselves, they should be willing to suffer wrong. They were to love their enemies, do good to those who hated them, bless those who cursed them, and pray for those who used them spitefully.
ch04.b081: Simon Zelotes wanted to spring to his feet. Turn the other cheek? When a Roman soldier shoved a fellow Jew off the road, when he saw neighbors stripped of their land by taxes, even then, turn the other cheek? Love your enemies? To a Zealot an enemy was not someone to love but someone to drive out. His face burned red. But he did not stand. Something in the Master’s face held him: that calm. That assurance, that poise, that composure no one could explain. It was the thing Simon admired in this man above all else. He had never in his life possessed such calm.
ch04.b082: The Father in heaven, the Master said, made his sun shine on the evil and the good, and sent his rain on the just and the unjust. They must be merciful as God is merciful. They had been commissioned to save men, he said, not to judge them. And they were not to go picking a speck out of a brother’s eye while a beam stayed lodged in their own.
ch04.b083: John’s face grew hot again. More than once in recent months he had stopped strangers who were teaching in the Master’s name. At the time he had thought it right. Now he thought about the beam in his own eye, and for the first time he suspected it might be rather large.
ch04.b084: The Master warned them against false prophets who would come in sheep’s clothing while inwardly they were ravening wolves. By their fruits they would be known. A good tree bore good fruit, he said, and a corrupt tree bore evil fruit. And in gaining entrance to the kingdom of heaven, it was the motive that counted. His Father looked into men’s hearts and judged them by their inner longings and their sincere intentions.
ch04.b085: As he listened, Judas Iscariot plucked at the blades of grass beside him. Motive. He tried to look into his own. But it was dark in there, and he did not know what he was meant to see. No; he did not want to see. He tossed the grass away and raised his head. The Master was not looking at him. Or was he? Judas could not be sure.
ch04.b086: At that moment Andrew was looking at Judas. The fingers plucking the grass, the angle at which he lifted his head. Andrew did not know what it meant. He only kept it in his memory.
ch04.b087: The Master spoke for a long time that afternoon. They had never heard such a voice from him. He had always been gentle, always patient, but today he spoke as one with supreme authority. Toward sundown they came down from the mountain. No one asked him a question. Not even Peter. Philip’s sack, still unopened, swung on his back all the way down.
ch04.b089: When they reached Zebedee’s house, they shared a simple meal. No one ate much. Only now did Philip’s barley loaves come out, and the twins broke them and passed them around. After the meal the Master went out to walk along the beach. The twelve stayed behind in the garden.
ch04.b090: For a while nobody spoke. Then Simon Zelotes broke the silence.
ch04.b091: “Turn the other cheek. Then when does Rome leave?”
ch04.b092: “Simon, what we heard today was about the kingdom, not about Rome.”
ch04.b093: Nathaniel said it gently. Simon glared at him but did not answer. Thomas sat hugging his knees and muttered:
ch04.b094: “He says don’t resist injustice by force, and then he tells us to show sound judgment and keen wisdom. He says don’t throw pearls before swine, and then he says love your enemies. I can’t see how these fit together.”
ch04.b096: Philip asked it honestly. No one answered. Judas Iscariot said in a low voice:
ch04.b097: “There must be something we don’t know. Something the Master hasn’t told us yet.”
ch04.b098: The words made the air in the garden a little colder. Matthew glanced at Judas. He could not read all that the words meant, but he felt that they had an edge. Matthew had dealt with men across a customs table for years; he knew the edge on a word when he heard it.
ch04.b100: Peter said it, and as usual that settled the matter. After a brief conference Andrew went out to find the Master. Meanwhile the twins built a small fire in the middle of the garden. The January night was cold, and a few lamps were not enough to let them see one another’s faces. When the dry sticks caught and began to crackle, the faces of eleven men rose out of the darkness in an orange glow.
ch04.b101: Andrew overtook the Master at the water’s edge. He told him frankly that his brethren could not understand what he had said about the kingdom, and that they did not feel able to begin this work until he had taught them more. He asked him to come back to the garden and help them grasp the meaning of his words. The Master went back with Andrew.
ch04.b102: He gathered them around the fire and taught them again. They found his message hard to take in, he said, because they wanted to build the new teaching directly on top of the old. They must be born again and begin afresh, like little children. But they must not suppose that he had come to set aside the law and the prophets. He had come not to destroy but to fulfill, to enlarge and to illuminate, and to write new commandments on the tablets of their hearts.
ch04.b103: Peter asked that if there was a new commandment, they might hear it; let him show them the new way. The Master took the commandment against killing and told them to look past the act to the motive. Anyone who was angry with his brother, anyone who nursed hatred in his heart and planned revenge, already stood in danger of judgment. Men must judge their fellows by their deeds, he said, but the Father in heaven judged by the intent.
ch04.b104: James Zebedee broke in to ask about divorce. Should they allow a man to divorce his wife, as Moses had? The Master said that he had come not to make laws but to enlighten, not to reform the kingdoms of this world but to establish the kingdom of heaven. It was not the Father’s will that he should teach them rules which might be good for today and yet would not suit another age. On divorce he said only this: that Moses had looked on it with favor, but it had not been so in the days of Adam and in the Garden.
ch04.b105: The apostles talked among themselves for a little while. Then the Master told them that every human act could be seen from two sides: the human and the divine, the way of the flesh and the way of the spirit, the reckoning of time and the view of eternity. They did not understand all of it. But it truly helped them. Things that had been jumbled together seemed now to be sorted onto two separate shelves. Thomas liked that.
ch04.b106: Nathaniel asked whether, then, there was to be no place at all for justice. The law of Moses said an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth; what were they to say to that? He had carried this question all afternoon. For an honest man, fairness was not something easily set aside.
ch04.b107: The Master told them to return good for evil. His messengers must not quarrel with men but be gentle toward all. Measure for measure must not be their rule. The rulers of men might keep such laws, but not so in the kingdom; there mercy would always decide their judgments, and love their conduct. And he added that if these were hard sayings, they could turn back even now. If they found the demands of apostleship too hard, they might return to the less rigorous path of discipleship.
ch04.b108: The fire snapped. No one seemed to breathe.
ch04.b109: The apostles got up and drew apart to a corner of the garden. In the dark beneath the fig tree they put their heads together. It did not take long.
ch04.b110: “I still don’t understand all of it.”
ch04.b112: “But I’ve no thought of turning back. If he weren’t the real thing, I’d have left long ago. My being here is my answer.”
ch04.b114: The twins said it almost together. The others nodded. Matthew said nothing. He had nowhere to go back to. No; he had somewhere, but he did not want to go there. Simon Zelotes nodded with his jaw set. His dream had been shaken many times that day, but the thought of leaving this man had not once crossed his mind. Judas nodded last. Andrew saw it.
ch04.b115: They soon came back, and Peter spoke for them all. They would go on with the Master, he said. Not one of them would turn back. They were ready to pay the greater price; they would drink the cup. They meant to be apostles, not merely disciples.
ch04.b116: Peter’s voice shook, but it was loud and clear. He had always been a man whose words ran ahead of him. But tonight his words did not run ahead of what was in their hearts. They were exactly what was in all their hearts. When he finished, his eyes were wet, and so were the eyes of the eleven men standing around the fire. Simon Zelotes held his fist against his chest. Thomas nodded. The twins were holding each other’s hands. Nathaniel, instead of joking, swallowed hard.
ch04.b117: Andrew looked at his brother. This time too, the words of praise would not come out of his throat. Instead he reached out and laid his hand on his brother’s shoulder, the way hands had been laid on his own head that afternoon on the highland. Peter turned and looked at him. Neither brother said anything. There was no need.
ch04.b118: It was an oath sworn beside a fire. That night Peter did not doubt a word of it. What the cup would be, what shape the price would take, he did not yet know. On a chilly night a little more than three years later, warming himself at a charcoal fire in a stranger’s courtyard, he would remember the fire of this night. But that night had not yet come. Tonight’s fire was warm, and his brother’s hand was on his shoulder.
ch04.b119: The Master looked at them one by one. There was joy in his eyes, and something deeper than joy: the look of one who knew when and where each of these promises would someday be shaken. Yet his look did not take the promise lightly at all. To receive a vow while knowing it would waver: that was the love they were given that night.
ch04.b120: Then, the Master said, let them gladly take up their responsibilities and follow him. Let them do their good deeds in secret; when they gave alms, the left hand was not to know what the right hand was doing. When they prayed, they were not to pile up empty repetitions, for the Father knew what they needed before they asked. They were not to store up treasure on earth but, by unselfish service, to store up treasure in heaven, because where their treasure was, there their hearts would be as well.
ch04.b121: Matthew took those words deep into his chest. Let not the left hand know what the right hand does. He was already doing that. But he wanted the Master to know. Let the left hand never know, so long as the Master did. He thought a long while about whether that wish went against these words, and he could not decide. What he hardly realized was that the Master had known all of it from the beginning.
ch04.b122: The lamp of the body was the eye, the Master said. If the eye was generous, the whole body would be full of light; if the eye was selfish, the whole body would be full of darkness. And if the very light within a man turned into darkness, how great that darkness would be.
ch04.b123: The firelight fell on one half of Judas Iscariot’s face. The other half lay buried in shadow. No one took any notice. It was only because of where the fire happened to be.
ch04.b125: Then Thomas asked whether they should go on holding everything in common. He was a man who had left a wife and four children at Tarichea. His was not a question of philosophy but of housekeeping.
ch04.b126: Yes, the Master said. He wished them to live together as one understanding family. A great work had been entrusted to them, and he longed for their undivided service. No man could serve two masters, he reminded them; no one could truly worship God and at the same time wholeheartedly serve mammon. So they were not to be anxious about what they would eat or drink, or what they would wear. They had already learned that willing hands and earnest hearts do not go hungry. If they sought the kingdom of God first, all they needed would be added to them. They were not to fret unduly over tomorrow; each day had trouble enough of its own.
ch04.b127: Judas Iscariot laid a hand on the purse in his lap. The common purse. It was his to guard. Do not be anxious about tomorrow; but being anxious about tomorrow was precisely his work. What thirteen men would eat next week, how much must go this month to the families waiting at home: someone had to work that out. The Master had not forbidden it. And yet in those words Judas felt his own work shrink a little. It irritated him. He did not let the irritation show on his face. He was skilled at such things.
ch04.b128: Philip heard the same words in another way. Do not worry about what you will eat. He was the steward, and worrying was his work. But he thought back over the past five months. Several times the food had nearly run out. It had almost never actually run out. From somewhere, something had always come. He did not know where it all came from. That a good share of it had come from the purse of Matthew, sitting right beside him, Philip would never know as long as he lived.
ch04.b129: The night deepened. Twice the fire sank low, and twice the twins coaxed it back. The apostles looked ready to sit up all night asking questions. When the Master saw it, he told them that they were earthen vessels; it would be best for them to go and rest, so as to be ready for the next day’s work.
ch04.b130: Earthen vessels. Nathaniel liked that. Easily broken, shaped from clay, and yet able to hold something. He thought of all they had been given to hold that day. The vessels were already running over.
ch04.b131: But sleep had gone from their eyes. No one got up.
ch04.b132: Peter was the first to find his courage. He asked whether he might have a little private talk with the Master. It was not that he wanted secrets from his brethren, he said, but his spirit was troubled, and if he deserved a rebuke, he could bear it better alone. It was a request quite unlike Peter. He was a man who said everything in front of everyone. But tonight he felt something shaking inside him, and he did not trust himself to show it before his brothers.
ch04.b133: The Master told Peter to come with him and led the way into the house.
ch04.b134: Those left in the garden watched the fire. Each of them pretended not to wonder what Peter was saying. Each of them wondered. After a while Peter came back. His face was not the face he had gone in with. It was the face of a man much cheered and greatly encouraged. He sat down by the fire without a word. Andrew looked at his brother’s face and saw there the best thing he had seen all day.
ch04.b135: Next James rose and went in. And so on through the early hours of the morning, the apostles went in one by one to talk with the Master.
ch04.b136: John went in and came out. He told no one what had been said. But afterward he sat a long while by the fire, leaning against his brother James’s shoulder. He was the youngest, and tonight he was not ashamed of being the youngest.
ch04.b137: Philip went in and came out. He came out nodding, like a man who has had something confirmed. Probably he had asked once more to be shown something, and probably the Master had once more, patiently, shown him.
ch04.b138: Nathaniel went in and came out. Coming out, for the first time that day, he smiled a little: the smile he had been holding back since morning.
ch04.b139: Matthew went in. Before he did, he hesitated a moment at the door. What would he say? Would he speak about the money? In the end he did not speak about the money. Coming out, he caught his foot on the threshold and stumbled, and Simon Zelotes, without thinking, caught him by the arm. For a moment the two men looked at each other. A publican and a Zealot. Simon let go first, but he did not let go roughly.
ch04.b140: Simon went in. He stayed a long time. When he came out, his face was as hard as ever, but the edge in his eyes had dulled a little.
ch04.b141: Thomas went in. He too stayed long; the Master enjoyed long talks with Thomas. When he came out, he sat by the fire and stared into it for a long time. It was not a face from which the doubt had gone. But it was the face of a man who had learned, a little, how to sit beside his doubt.
ch04.b142: Judas Iscariot went in. Before he did, he straightened his clothes; that was his habit. He stayed neither long nor short. When he came out, his face was almost the same as when he had gone in. No one found that strange. Judas’s face was always like that. Only Andrew looked at it a second time. And he could read nothing there at all. That, more than anything, left him uneasy.
ch04.b144: The twins, meanwhile, had fallen asleep. They lay side by side by the fire, their heads tilted at the same angle, breathing in the same rhythm. Someone had spread a cloak over them. Probably Nathaniel.
ch04.b145: Andrew went in last to talk with the Master. He was the chief, and the chief checks last. When every one of them had had his private conference except the twins, Andrew went in to the Master once more and told him that the twins had fallen asleep in the garden by the fire. Should he wake them, he asked, to see whether they too wished to talk with him?
ch04.b146: The Master smiled. They were doing well, he told Andrew; let them be.
ch04.b147: Andrew went back into the garden and stood beside the twins. The fire had burned nearly out; only red embers were left. There was no worry at all in the twins’ faces. All day long they had fully understood nothing. And they had lost nothing. Andrew stood a long while thinking about what that meant. Some men came to the Master with questions, and some came with sleep. The Master received them both.
ch04.b148: He looked around the garden. Peter was dozing against the wall. John was still leaning on James’s shoulder. Philip lay with his empty sack for a pillow. Matthew and Simon sat on opposite sides of the fire, each looking away, but not as far apart as they would once have sat. Thomas was still awake; he saw Andrew and gave a small nod. Nathaniel was asleep and murmuring something. Probably he was making jokes even in his dreams.
ch04.b149: Judas Iscariot sat alone beneath the fig tree at the far end of the garden. He was not asleep. The purse was still on his knee. He was watching the eastern sky. For a moment Andrew thought of going over to him. But what would he say? He did not know how to praise, and he hardly knew how to comfort. And he could not even tell whether what he wanted to say to Judas now was praise, or comfort, or a warning. He did not go. Whether that was right, he would not know for a long, long time.
ch04.b150: The night was passing. Over the hills beyond the Sea of Galilee, the light of another day was spreading thinly. It was the same light as the morning before. But the twelve men beneath it were not the twelve of the morning before. They were ambassadors of the kingdom now. Even they did not yet know all that this meant. They knew only the memory of cold earth on their knees, and the weight of the hands that had rested on their heads. It was a weight they would never forget as long as they lived. One of them would, in the end, lay it down; but at that dawn no one knew it. Only one knew: the one who had laid his hands on them all.
ch04.b152: The course of events follows Paper 140, “The Ordination of the Twelve”: the morning call by the lake and the climb into the highlands north of Capernaum (140:0.1–0.3); the teaching before the ordination (140:1.1–1.7); the laying on of hands, beginning with Judas Iscariot and ending with Andrew, the prayer, and the silent embraces (140:2.1–2.3); the ordination sermon and the descent at sundown (140:3.1–3.21); and the evening questions in the garden of Zebedee’s house, the vow by the fire, the private conferences, and the sleeping twins (140:6.1–6.14).
ch04.b153: The apostles’ ages, families, characters, and duties come from Paper 139 (139:0.3, 139:1–12); the choosing and organizing of the twelve, Judas’s question about John’s imprisonment, and Jesus’ words to Judas at Tarichea come from Paper 138 (138:2–10). Matthew’s secret support of the apostolic funds (139:7.8–7.9), Andrew’s unspoken awareness of trouble in Judas (139:1.8), the death of Thomas’s twin sister when he was nine (139:8.10), and John’s forbidding of strangers who taught in Jesus’ name (139:4.8) rest on the text.
ch04.b154: Added fiction includes the apostles’ inner thoughts and feelings; weather, landscape, and sensory detail; the brief exchanges among the apostles (Nathaniel’s joke about lunch, the words of Simon, Thomas, Philip, and Judas in the garden, the talk under the fig tree); Philip’s sack and barley loaves; Matthew and Simon meeting at the doorway; the faces of each man after his private talk; the particular manner of each embrace; and Andrew’s hand on his brother’s shoulder. The foreshadowing of Peter by the charcoal fire in Annas’s courtyard (184:2) and of Thomas meeting these hands again behind barred doors (191:5) looks ahead to later chapters. What Jesus said in the private conferences is not recorded, and nothing has been invented for it. The order in which the hands passed between Judas and Andrew is the novel’s own.
ch04.b155: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
